edits.old: MongoDB groups measurements into a bucket only when their metaField values match and their timeField values are close. Its manual says bucket count depends on the number of unique metaField values and that fine-grained or dynamic values can produce sparse, short-lived buckets with lower storage and query efficiency. This is a scoped risk rather than a universal failure rule: the manual also says compressed time-series workloads can support high cardinality. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

evidence.quote: Because `metaField` values must match exactly to group documents, the number of buckets in a time series collection depends on the number of unique `metaField` values.
Collections with fine-grained or changing `metaField` values generate many sparsely packed, short-lived buckets. This leads to decreased storage and query efficiency.

Compressing time series data in the cache supports high [cardinality](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-cardinality) workloads while preserving efficient query performance.

edits.rationale: The bucketing page states that buckets group documents with identical metaField values and close timeField values, that bucket count depends on unique metaField values, and that fine-grained or changing values give sparse, short-lived buckets with lower efficiency. The high-cardinality statement is not on the bucketing page. It is on the sibling Time Series Collections Considerations page of the same manual, which says compressing time series data in the cache supports high cardinality workloads.
